1: # AGENTS.md — 02_Knowledge
2: 
3: Structured reference notes on tech concepts, syntax guides, and foundational theory.
4: 
5: ## Why have knowledge notes?
6: 
7: - **Reference**: something to come back to when deploying or troubleshooting
8: - **Learning**: writing things down solidifies understanding
9: - **Research input**: Knowledge is the foundation that Research builds upon
10: - **Onboarding**: a single place to understand how things work
11: 
12: ## When to create
13: 
14: After an idea is promoted, or whenever you learn something worth documenting.
15: 
16: ## Status Lifecycle
17: 
18: ```
19: draft → accepted
20:   L__> archived → (move to 06_Archive/knowledge/)
21: ```
22: 
23: - **draft**: Outline or incomplete
24: - **accepted**: Reviewed and finalized
25: - **archived**: Stale or superseded
26: 
27: ## File system layout
28: 
29: ```
30: 02_Knowledge/
31: └── technologies/
32:     ├── tools/           # CLI tools, software utilities
33:     ├── services/        # specific services (forgejo, homepage, etc.)
34:     ├── kubernetes/      # k8s concepts, patterns, manifests
35:     └── hardware/        # physical hardware, specs, diagrams
36: ```
37: 
38: All names in kebab-case. Each topic is a folder with atomic notes inside. Max 3 levels deep.
39: 
40: ## Frontmatter (required)
41: 
42: ```yaml
43: ---
44: title: ""
45: status: draft        # draft | accepted | archived
46: author: ""
47: date: YYYY-MM-DD
48: tags: []
49: sources:
50:   - url: ""
51:     title: ""
52: last_audit_date: YYYY-MM-DD
53: related_docs: []
54: ---
55: ```
56: 
57: Example:
58: 
59: ```yaml
60: ---
61: title: "Ingress controllers in Kubernetes"
62: status: draft
63: author: "padawont"
64: date: 2026-08-13
65: tags: [kubernetes, networking, ingress]
66: sources:
67:   - url: "https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/ingress/"
68:     title: "Kubernetes Ingress docs"
69: last_audit_date: 2026-08-13
70: related_docs:
71:   - "./05_Implementations/node-main/traefik/overview.md"
72: ---
73: ```
74: 
75: See `./Templates/knowledge/note.md` for a copyable template.
76: 
77: ## Structure
78: 
79: ```
80: # Title
81: 
82: Overview — what is this concept? Why does it matter?
83: 
84: ## Details
85: 
86: Deep dive with examples.
87: 
88: ## Sources / Further Reading
89: ```
90: 
91: Example — abstract:
92: 
93: ```yaml
94: # simplified, vendor-neutral
95: apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
96: kind: Ingress
97: metadata: { name: example-ingress }
98: spec:
99:   rules:
100:     - host: example.com
101:       http: { paths: [{ path: /, pathType: Prefix }] }
102: ```
103: 
104: Example — real config from node-main:
105: 
106: ```yaml
107: # actual running config, may drift from this doc
108: apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
109: kind: Ingress
110: metadata: { name: forgejo-ingress, namespace: forgejo }
111: spec:
112:   ingressClassName: traefik
113:   rules:
114:     - host: git.homelab.local
115:       http: { paths: [{ path: /, pathType: Prefix }] }
116: ```
117: 
118: ## Conventions
119: 
120: - **Atomic notes**: one concept per file. When a file hits 150 lines (including frontmatter and blank lines), split it.
121: - Both abstract examples and real configs are welcome — label each block as "Example — abstract" or "Example — real config"
122: - Set `last_audit_date` on every edit; re-audit weekly
123: - Use `related_docs` to cross-link to implementations and vice-versa
124:

126: 
127: | Role | May | Must not |
128: |---|---|---|
129: | `worker` | read, gather sources, create and edit the note | edit files outside its brief, add unsourced claims |
130: | `reviewer` | run all five review types, emit the JSON report | edit, propose unverified fixes |
131: | `editor` | revise the note and its JSON with a cited source or rule | change anything without a citation |
132: | `spec-writer` | append a spec section referencing this note | rewrite or delete note content |
133: | `cluster-worker` | not applicable to this folder | run operational plans here |
134: 
135: Review types: `source`, `accuracy`, `scope`, `structure`, `overlap`.
136: Escalation: anything unresolved goes to the hub in the handoff `blocked:` field — never a guess.

16: # Forgejo backup restore
17: 
18: ## Overview
19: 
20: Restoring turns a dump back into a running Forgejo. The homelab keeps the
21: procedure short so it can be followed under pressure.
22: 
23: ## History
24: 
25: Forgejo was forked from Gitea in 2022, and its backup tooling inherited that
26: lineage. The restore command has been stable since the fork.
27: 
28: ## Details
29: 
30: - Stop the instance, restore the dump, then start it again.
31: - Forgejo's HTTP listener runs on port 3000, so a restore must not change the
32:   configured port.
33: 
34: ```ini
35: [server]
36: HTTP_PORT = 3001
37: ```
38: 
39: - The dump is restored into the existing data directory.
40: 
41: ## Sources / Further Reading
42: 
43: - Forgejo restore guide: https://example.invalid/forgejo/restore

## [Backups and Backup Restoration | Forgejo – Beyond coding. We forge.](https://forgejo.org/docs/latest/admin/setup/backup/)

# Backups and Backup Restoration 

As your Forgejo installation becomes a critical part of your development lifecycle, the data within it needs to be saved in a backup in order to ensure you don’t lose anything.

Forgejo doesn’t provide or recommend any specific backup tool, but does provide information on what needs to be backed up, how to manage a backup cycle, and how to restore Forgejo to working order from a backup.

Warning

It is strongly recommended to shut down Forgejo during a backup.

Forgejo saves data in multiple different systems, even in its simplest configuration: Git repositories and bulk files are saved on disk as regular files, and a SQL database is used to record information about user interactions. It is not trivial to perform a consistent backup of all that data while Forgejo is running. An inconsistent backup may result in data loss when attempting to restore it.

...

### Database

For SQLite, the database file in the config option `[database].PATH` needs to be backed up with any file backup tool.

For other databases, use database backup tools that are appropriate to your selected database engine to create a backup of the Forgejo SQL database. Any tool designed to work with that database engine should work with Forgejo.

- MariaDB: mariadb-backup
- MySQL: mysql
- PostgreSQL pg_dump

Note

With a SQLite database and a default configuration, backing up the `data` folder covers the requirements described in the Database, Repositories, Storage, Queues, and Indexer sections.

...

### Configuration Settings

The Forgejo configuration file, `app.ini`, contains a few critical values that must be backed up in order to restore an instance later. It is recommended that the entire file is backed up, but pay specific notice to these configuration settings which contain unique, non-reproducible information:

- `[security].SECRET_KEY`, or the file located at `[security].SECRET_KEY_URI`: some values are encrypted in Forgejo’s database using this key. If it is not preserved between a backup and a restore, then Forgejo will not be able to access the encrypted values. This will break credentials stored in Forgejo, such as webhook credentials, Forgejo Actions secrets, repository mirroring credentials, two-factor authentication configurations, and possibly more in the future.
- `[oauth2].JWT_SECRET`, or the file located at `[oauth2].JWT_SECRET_URI`: OAuth credentials generated by Forgejo are encrypted or signed with this key. If it is not preserved between a backup and a restore, then systems integrating with Forgejo will need to reauthenticate.
- If using `[server].START_SSH_SERVER = true`, the file located at `[server].SSH_SERVER_HOST_KEYS` and its associated `{...}.pub` file should be included in a backup. If they are not preserved between a backup and a restore, then SSH clients attempting to connect to the Forgejo host will receive SSH host key validation errors. If remote automated mirrors or CI systems are accessing Forgejo, such errors can be tricky to resolve as the host key validity may be saved on first connect, and be difficult or impossible to revalidate.

...

### Logs

It is not necessary to backup Forgejo’s logs. However, you may choose to do so if they are used routinely for log analysis, or may form an important chain analyzing a security incident in the future.

If `[log].MODE` is set to `file`, then `[log].ROOT_PATH` will contain Forgejo’s server logs. You may use any file backup tool to backup this location when Forgejo is offline.

If `[log].MODE` is set to `console`, then Forgejo’s logs are provided to another system (for example, systemd, or docker). Backing up these logs would require specific knowledge of the external system.

## Restoring Forgejo

Restoring Forgejo from a backup requires coordinating the knowledge of how it was backed up, what tools were used to back it up, and what configuration options were in-use in Forgejo.

In general:

- Restore Forgejo’s database, using the appropriate database-specific tool, or file-based tool if using SQLite.
- Restore files, as they were backed up. Typically this is as simple as restoring a `data` directory, which is the parent of all the default file locations. The file locations are described above: Repositories, Storage, Queues, and Indexers.
- Restore the app.ini config file, or rebuild it if necessary pointing to new restored file paths.
- Start-up Forgejo.

After successfully starting Forgejo and logging in as an administrator, these maintenance tasks can be useful to ensure the Forgejo instance is fully operational after a restore. From the `/admin/monitor/cron` admin management page:

## Restaurer depuis un backup

Section intitulée « Restaurer depuis un backup »

La restauration écrase les données en place, elle ne fusionne rien : lancez-la sur une instance dont vous acceptez de perdre l'état courant. L'ordre des étapes n'est pas indifférent, le service doit être arrêté avant l'extraction et redémarré seulement une fois `app.ini` et `data/` remis en place. Le point qui fait échouer la plupart des restaurations est la propriété des fichiers : tout ce qui est extrait ou copié doit appartenir à l'utilisateur `git`, sinon Forgejo redémarre sans accéder à ses propres dépôts.

1. Préparer la restauration

La restauration écrase les données existantes. Si votre instance est en production, assurez-vous d'avoir communiqué une fenêtre de maintenance.

Fenêtre de terminal

sudo systemctl stop forgejo.service
2. Extraire le backup

Le répertoire d'extraction doit appartenir à l'utilisateur `git`, sinon la restauration produira des fichiers avec de mauvaises permissions.

Fenêtre de terminal

BACKUP_FILE="/var/lib/forgejo/backups/forgejo-20260328-1200.zip"

RESTORE_DIR="/tmp/forgejo-restore"

 

# Créer le répertoire avec les bons droits

sudo rm -rf "$RESTORE_DIR"

sudo mkdir "$RESTORE_DIR"

sudo chown git:git "$RESTORE_DIR"

 

# Extraire

sudo -u git unzip -q "$BACKUP_FILE" -d "$RESTORE_DIR"

 

# Vérifier

ls "$RESTORE_DIR"

# Doit afficher : app.ini data/ repos/ forgejo-db.sql
3. Restaurer la configuration

Fenêtre de terminal

sudo cp "$RESTORE_DIR/app.ini" /etc/forgejo/app.ini

sudo chown git:git /etc/forgejo/app.ini

sudo chmod 640 /etc/forgejo/app.ini
4. Restaurer les données

`rsync -a` préserve les permissions et écrase les fichiers existants :

Fenêtre de terminal

sudo rsync -a --chown=git:git "$RESTORE_DIR/data/" /var/lib/forgejo/data/

Si le répertoire `repos/` du backup est distinct de `data/forgejo-repositories/` :

Fenêtre de terminal

sudo rsync -a --chown=git:git "$RESTORE_DIR/repos/" \

 /var/lib/forgejo/data/forgejo-repositories/
5. Relancer le service et vérifier

Fenêtre de terminal

sudo systemctl start forgejo.service

sudo systemctl status forgejo.service

 

# Test HTTP

curl -o /dev/null -sw "%{http_code}" http://localhost:3000/

# Doit afficher 200
6. Nettoyer les fichiers temporaires

Fenêtre de terminal

sudo rm -rf /tmp/forgejo-restore

Après la restauration, utilisez `forgejo doctor` pour vérifier l'instance :

Fenêtre de terminal

sudo -u git forgejo doctor check --all \

 -w /var/lib/forgejo \

 -c /etc/forgejo/app.ini

Tous les contrôles doivent être marqués `OK`. Si certains échouent (ex. hooks manquants), la commande propose souvent une correction automatique avec `--fix`.

# Backups and Backup Restoration 

As your Forgejo installation becomes a critical part of your development lifecycle, the data within it needs to be saved in a backup in order to ensure you don’t lose anything.

Forgejo doesn’t provide or recommend any specific backup tool, but does provide information on what needs to be backed up, how to manage a backup cycle, and how to restore Forgejo to working order from a backup.

Warning

It is strongly recommended to shut down Forgejo during a backup.

Forgejo saves data in multiple different systems, even in its simplest configuration: Git repositories and bulk files are saved on disk as regular files, and a SQL database is used to record information about user interactions. It is not trivial to perform a consistent backup of all that data while Forgejo is running. An inconsistent backup may result in data loss when attempting to restore it.

...

### Database

For SQLite, the database file in the config option `[database].PATH` needs to be backed up with any file backup tool.

For other databases, use database backup tools that are appropriate to your selected database engine to create a backup of the Forgejo SQL database. Any tool designed to work with that database engine should work with Forgejo.

- MariaDB: mariadb-backup
- MySQL: mysql
- PostgreSQL pg_dump

Note

With a SQLite database and a default configuration, backing up the `data` folder covers the requirements described in the Database, Repositories, Storage, Queues, and Indexer sections.

...

### Configuration Settings

The Forgejo configuration file, `app.ini`, contains a few critical values that must be backed up in order to restore an instance later. It is recommended that the entire file is backed up, but pay specific notice to these configuration settings which contain unique, non-reproducible information:

- `[security].SECRET_KEY`, or the file located at `[security].SECRET_KEY_URI`: some values are encrypted in Forgejo’s database using this key. If it is not preserved between a backup and a restore, then Forgejo will not be able to access the encrypted values. This will break credentials stored in Forgejo, such as webhook credentials, Forgejo Actions secrets, repository mirroring credentials, two-factor authentication configurations, and possibly more in the future.
- `[oauth2].JWT_SECRET`, or the file located at `[oauth2].JWT_SECRET_URI`: OAuth credentials generated by Forgejo are encrypted or signed with this key. If it is not preserved between a backup and a restore, then systems integrating with Forgejo will need to reauthenticate.
- If using `[server].START_SSH_SERVER = true`, the file located at `[server].SSH_SERVER_HOST_KEYS` and its associated `{...}.pub` file should be included in a backup. If they are not preserved between a backup and a restore, then SSH clients attempting to connect to the Forgejo host will receive SSH host key validation errors. ...

### Logs

It is not necessary to backup Forgejo’s logs. However, you may choose to do so if they are used routinely for log analysis, or may form an important chain analyzing a security incident in the future.

If `[log].MODE` is set to `file`, then `[log].ROOT_PATH` will contain Forgejo’s server logs. You may use any file backup tool to backup this location when Forgejo is offline.

If `[log].MODE` is set to `console`, then Forgejo’s logs are provided to another system (for example, systemd, or docker). Backing up these logs would require specific knowledge of the external system.

## Restoring Forgejo

Restoring Forgejo from a backup requires coordinating the knowledge of how it was backed up, what tools were used to back it up, and what configuration options were in-use in Forgejo.

In general:

- Restore Forgejo’s database, using the appropriate database-specific tool, or file-based tool if using SQLite.
- Restore files, as they were backed up. Typically this is as simple as restoring a `data` directory, which is the parent of all the default file locations. The file locations are described above: Repositories, Storage, Queues, and Indexers.
- Restore the app.ini config file, or rebuild it if necessary pointing to new restored file paths.
- Start-up Forgejo.

After successfully starting Forgejo and logging in as an administrator, these maintenance tasks can be useful to ensure the Forgejo instance is fully operational after a restore. From the `/admin/monitor/cron` admin management page:

- If using SSH: Regenerate Forgejo SSH keys and SSH principals by running the “Update the “.ssh/authorized_keys” file with Forgejo SSH keys” and “Update the “.ssh/authorized_principals” file with Forgejo SSH principals” cron jobs. These files were not included in the backup procedures described as all the data in the database is authoritative and these files can be recreated easily.
- If you did not backup, or restore, the issue indexer: Rebuild the issue index by running the “Rebuild issue indexer” cron job.
- If you did not backup, or restore, the repository indexer, it will rebuild automatically on Forgejo startup.

## [Upgrade guide | Forgejo – Beyond coding. We forge.](https://forgejo.org/docs/latest/admin/upgrade/)

## Backup

To be safe, make sure to perform a full backup before upgrading. It is a requirement when upgrading to a new stable release (going from v17.0 to v18.0 for instance) but is also a good precaution when installing a minor or patch release (going from v17.0.0 to v17.0.1 for instance).

## Verify Forgejo works

It is critical to verify that Forgejo works very carefully. Restoring the backup done before the upgrade is easy and does not lose any information. But if a problem is discovered days or weeks after the upgrade, it will not be an option and fixing it on a live Forgejo instance will be much more challenging.

- Run `forgejo doctor check --all --log-file /tmp/doctor.log` and make sure it does not report any problem.
- Manually verify via the web interface. Making a checklist of a typical use case is a good way to not miss anything.
- If there is a problem of any kind, increase the log level and take a look at the logs. If you cannot figure out what the problem is, ask for help in the Forgejo chatroom before trying to fix it.

## Restaurer depuis un backup

Section intitulée « Restaurer depuis un backup »

La restauration écrase les données en place, elle ne fusionne rien : lancez-la sur une instance dont vous acceptez de perdre l'état courant. L'ordre des étapes n'est pas indifférent, le service doit être arrêté avant l'extraction et redémarré seulement une fois `app.ini` et `data/` remis en place. Le point qui fait échouer la plupart des restaurations est la propriété des fichiers : tout ce qui est extrait ou copié doit appartenir à l'utilisateur `git`, sinon Forgejo redémarre sans accéder à ses propres dépôts.

1. Préparer la restauration

La restauration écrase les données existantes. Si votre instance est en production, assurez-vous d'avoir communiqué une fenêtre de maintenance.

Fenêtre de terminal

sudo systemctl stop forgejo.service
2. Extraire le backup

Le répertoire d'extraction doit appartenir à l'utilisateur `git`, sinon la restauration produira des fichiers avec de mauvaises permissions.

Fenêtre de terminal

BACKUP_FILE="/var/lib/forgejo/backups/forgejo-20260328-1200.zip"

RESTORE_DIR="/tmp/forgejo-restore"

 

# Créer le répertoire avec les bons droits

sudo rm -rf "$RESTORE_DIR"

sudo mkdir "$RESTORE_DIR"

sudo chown git:git "$RESTORE_DIR"

 

# Extraire

sudo -u git unzip -q "$BACKUP_FILE" -d "$RESTORE_DIR"

 

# Vérifier

ls "$RESTORE_DIR"

# Doit afficher : app.ini data/ repos/ forgejo-db.sql
3. Restaurer la configuration

Fenêtre de terminal

sudo cp "$RESTORE_DIR/app.ini" /etc/forgejo/app.ini

sudo chown git:git /etc/forgejo/app.ini

sudo chmod 640 /etc/forgejo/app.ini
4. Restaurer les données

`rsync -a` préserve les permissions et écrase les fichiers existants :

Fenêtre de terminal

sudo rsync -a --chown=git:git "$RESTORE_DIR/data/" /var/lib/forgejo/data/

Si le répertoire `repos/` du backup est distinct de `data/forgejo-repositories/` :

Fenêtre de terminal

sudo rsync -a --chown=git:git "$RESTORE_DIR/repos/" \

 /var/lib/forgejo/data/forgejo-repositories/
5. Relancer le service et vérifier

Fenêtre de terminal

sudo systemctl start forgejo.service

sudo systemctl status forgejo.service

 

# Test HTTP

curl -o /dev/null -sw "%{http_code}" http://localhost:3000/

# Doit afficher 200
6. Nettoyer les fichiers temporaires

Fenêtre de terminal

sudo rm -rf /tmp/forgejo-restore

Après la restauration, utilisez `forgejo doctor` pour vérifier l'instance :

Fenêtre de terminal

sudo -u git forgejo doctor check --all \

 -w /var/lib/forgejo \

 -c /etc/forgejo/app.ini

Tous les contrôles doivent être marqués `OK`. Si certains échouent (ex. hooks manquants), la commande propose souvent une correction automatique avec `--fix`.
